I think this law is not really a local issue, but state-wide. Banning lead was a really good initiative by California. The problem is it's stupid to enforce, and it makes things more expensive to produce, even if they're already lead-free. I made a few examples in a reply to /u/thepower just above this.

Lead itself and its history in regards to manufacturing and industry is pretty awful. It's just extremely cheap to produce, and it's easy to use for a variety of applications. It has been used in so many things over the last few centuries it's almost a miracle anyone survived.

Clair Cameron Patterson was the man who first noticed in the late 1940's that the entire world's population was being lead-poisoned. He was busy working on a way to date how old the earth/universe was accurately. He figured out that uranium naturally decayed into lead at a predictable rate, and thought he could work backwards to find the age of the earth/universe by measuring current lead levels in different rocks/meteorites. He kept having this problem where all his samples had way more lead than they should, no matter where the sample came from. He eventually figured out it was the air itself that was contaminating his samples.

The culprit for atmospheric lead was Tetraethyllead, a product sold by the Ethyl Corporation "in the 1920s as a patented octane rating booster". The Ethyl Corporation was started by the usual suspects: a few American auto manufacturers and the Rothschild's Standard Oil. They spent the next 5 decades defending their patented product and black-balling Patterson in every endeavor possible. Patterson had all his funding removed and was even refused contracts by the US Public Health Service.

It took until 1986 before the United States would fully phase-out Tetraethyllead. It is still being sold to 3rd world countries to this day, and continues to be used as an additive in some aviation fuels.

Patterson would also prove, by testing the bones of ancient mummies and comparing them to the bones of modern people, that people alive between 1920-1990 had 700 to 1200 times the amount of lead in their bodies compared to any previous time. Atmospheric lead levels have been dropping quickly since the 1990's, but we're not really sure how lasting the effects will be.

Anyways I could go on for a while, so I'll encourage anyone who is further interested in this stuff do some research of their own. The point is California is not crazy for wanting to force industries to prove their products are lead-free, it's just the catch 22 of a lot of government programs.
